title: Help these women (Philippians 4:1–3)
hook: Euodia and Syntyche, co-workers, are asked to agree

segments.voice: Yesterday, a runner pressing toward the mark, and your line was forgetting what's behind, reaching forth.

Two names, and that's almost all we know: Euodia and Syntyche. Paul's letter will be read aloud to the whole church at Philippi, and in the middle of it he names two women who aren't getting along. We don't know what the quarrel was about. Money, a meeting, a hurt word, a plan for the church. The letter never says, and it's honest to leave it there. What we do know is how Paul handles it. He doesn't take a side. He doesn't send a rebuke. He asks for help.

First he speaks to the whole church with real warmth: they are, in the King James Bible, "my joy and crown." Then: "I beseech Euodias, and beseech Syntyche, that they be of the same mind in the Lord." He says beseech twice, once to each woman. Neither is named first as the problem. And same mind is a phrase from all through this letter: be likeminded, let this mind be in you. It doesn't mean agreeing on every detail. It means facing the same direction. Then he turns to someone else: "And I intreat thee also, true yokefellow, help those women which laboured with me in the gospel." Who is the yokefellow? Nobody knows. Some think it's a friend Paul doesn't name. Some think Syzygos, Greek for yokefellow, was the man's actual name. Either way, a third person is asked to help two people find their way back. And look how Paul describes these women: not as troublemakers, but as co-workers who labored with him in the gospel, along with Clement and the rest, "whose names are in the book of life." Their quarrel doesn't cancel their work. Philippi's church began, Acts says, with women at a place of prayer by a river, and Lydia opening her home. Women were there from the start. This week has walked through Philippians: look to others, he emptied himself, shine like stars, two helpers honored, counting it loss, press on, and now two co-workers asked to agree.
screen: `CO-WORKERS, NAMES IN THE BOOK OF LIFE.`
then, large: `BE OF THE SAME MIND IN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Think of two people you know who have drifted apart or fallen out, friends, siblings, coworkers, and don't decide who's right; Paul didn't. Picture each of them and remember one good thing each has done, then ask whether there's a small way to help without taking sides, even just by not feeding the quarrel. If you pray, you can hold both of them before God by name.
Syzygos. Greek for yokefellow, one who pulls in the same yoke, maybe even the man's own name: Paul's friend, asked to help Euodia and Syntyche find the same mind again.
Your line: be of one mind. Facing the same direction, not agreeing on everything. A week of Philippians, done.

howItsDone: Many churches ask a trusted third person, a pastor, elder or friend, to help members reconcile, and some read Philippians 4:2–3 when teaching about peacemaking in the congregation.

chat.says: Two women in Paul's church were quarreling. Whose side did he take?
options: Neither. He begged each by name to be of one mind, and asked a friend to help.
Euodia's, because he named her first and called the other one stubborn.
Neither, so he told the church to put them both out until they agreed.
chat.meaning: Paul says "I beseech" to each woman, takes no side, and asks his true yokefellow to help them.

notes: The KJV spells the first name 'Euodias'; the Greek is Euodia (a woman's name). The script says Euodia in its own voice and quotes the KJV spelling.
Identity of the 'true yokefellow' (σύζυγε, vocative) is unknown; the proper-name reading is a minority but long-standing suggestion. Confirm.
